title: Evaluating Quantum Kernel Methods for Track-Based Classification in High-Energy Physics
abstract: We present a systematic design for large-scale quantum kernel classification, demonstrated through a quantum support vector classifier (QSVC) for particle-track classification using centroid-based CLAS12 drift-chamber features. Each event is encoded into a six-qubit state via a fully entangled ZZFeatureMap, whose fidelities define a quantum kernel within a standard SVM framework. By decoupling state preparation from kernel construction and distributing evaluation across a multi-node MPI-based HPC allocation, the approach scales to 1.0x10^5 training and 4.0x10^5 test events with an exactly constructed kernel matrix, to our knowledge more than an order of magnitude larger than prior high-energy-physics quantum-kernel studies.   Benchmarked against linear, polynomial, RBF, and sigmoid SVM kernels and extremely randomized trees (ERT), the ideal QSVC achieves the highest recall (99.99%) among all models. Under a calibrated hardware noise model (FakeMumbaiV2, 500 training / 2,000 test events), AUC falls from 0.9985 to 0.9671 and peak significance improvement falls from 17.5 to ~3.5, yet recall remains at 99.51% -- indicating this signal-retention advantage is attenuated but not eliminated by circuit-level decoherence.   Geometric analysis of the quantum embedding shows near-orthogonal inter-class states with coherent intra-class neighborhoods under ideal simulation; under noise this structure compresses toward the maximally mixed state while preserving its relative ordering.   These results demonstrate a scalable, reproducible workflow for quantum kernel experimentation at HEP-relevant scale, quantifying the practical cost of realistic hardware noise on quantum-enhanced classification.
summary: This work presents a scalable framework for applying Quantum Support Vector Classifiers to particle-track identification in HEP. By encoding detector features into a quantum state, the authors demonstrate that the quantum kernel maintains a critical advantage in signal retention over classical methods, even when accounting for realistic hardware decoherence.
main_problem: The paper evaluates the utility of quantum kernel methods for distinguishing particle tracks from background noise in high-energy physics (HEP) data.
main_result: The Quantum Support Vector Classifier (QSVC) achieved the highest recall (99.99%) in ideal simulations, demonstrating a signal-retention advantage over classical methods, which persists even under realistic hardware noise.
method: A quantum kernel is constructed using a fully entangled ZZFeatureMap, which is then integrated into a standard Support Vector Machine (SVM) framework for classification.
model_or_system: The system is particle-track classification using centroid-based features from the CLAS12 drift-chamber detector. The methodology involves simulating the quantum kernel computation on large datasets using multi-node HPC resources.
key_observables: Recall (99.99% ideal, 99.51% noisy), AUC (0.9985 ideal, 0.9671 noisy), and peak significance improvement.
important_parameters: Scales up to $4.0 	imes 10^5$ test events; performance is quantified under a calibrated hardware noise model (FakeMumbaiV2).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the quantum kernel's ability to capture non-linear correlations provides a distinct advantage in signal-retention, even when hardware noise degrades performance.
figures_summary: The notes suggest geometric analysis showing near-orthogonal inter-class states under ideal conditions, and performance curves comparing ideal vs. noisy metrics.
paper_structure: The paper systematically designs the QSVC workflow, benchmarks it against classical kernels (linear, RBF, etc.), and then rigorously tests its performance under both ideal simulation and realistic hardware noise models.
why_interesting: While the application is HEP, the core methodology—quantifying the performance gap between ideal quantum computation and noisy, scalable quantum kernel estimation—is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Wire activations in a drift-chamber superlayer produced by a traversing charged particle. Activated segments (left) and individual hit cells (right) illustrate the spatial structure from which centroid-based features are derived [5].

Figure 2: ROC diagnostics comparing the QSVC with classical baselines. Left: Global ROC curves show that ERT achieves the highest AUC (0.9994), while the ideal QSVC (AUC 0.9985) exhibits a near-vertical rise from the origin consistent with its near-zero false-negative rate. The noisy QSVC (AUC 0.9671) shows a markedly slower rise, reflecting degraded background rejection under hardware noise. Right: Optimal operating points illustrate the complementary trade-offs between the two strongest ideal models: ERT maximises precision and specificity while the QSVC maximises recall; the noisy QSVC’s operating point sits well outside this cluster, quantifying the performance cost of circuit- level...

Figure 3: Physics-motivated performance diagnostics comparing the ideal QSVC, noisy QSVC, and ERT. (a) Background rejection curves show that ERT leads the ideal QSVC across nearly the entire efficiency range; the noisy QSVC’s rejection curve sits well below both. (b) The ideal QSVC’s SIC maximum occurs at much higher signal efficiency than ERT’s, though at a lower absolute value; ERT’s peak is higher but narrower and more sen- sitive to threshold choice. The noisy QSVC’s flattened, low-amplitude SIC curve indicates that hardware noise degrades not only peak significance but also the threshold-tunability that makes a classifier operationally useful.

Figure 4: Visualizations of the quantum feature space produced by the ZZFeatureMap. Left: PCA shows that although the embedding is highly expressive, its nonlinear struc- ture cannot be captured by linear projections. Right: t-SNE reveals meaningful geometric organization, with signal and background forming intertwined but locally distinguishable regions. Together, these projections illustrate that the quantum kernel induces a smooth, nonlinear manifold structure that enables the QSVC to construct a sharp decision bound- ary in the full Hilbert space.

Figure 5: Quantum-state structure induced by the ZZFeatureMap under ideal simula- tion. Left: Entanglement entropy characterises the expressivity of the static feature-map encoding. Right: Fidelity distributions reveal that inter-class states tend toward near- orthogonality while intra-class states retain coherent local neighbourhoods, consistent with the ideal QSVC’s decision-boundary geometry. A quantitative, ideal-versus-noisy compar- ison of this fidelity structure is presented in Section 7.3.
